newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbian opposition keeps up pressure on Milosevic.
newsitem.headline: Serbian opposition keeps up pressure on Milosevic.

text.p: Serbia's opposition, leading a wave of popular outrage against President Slobodan Milosevic, planned new initiatives on Sunday in a campaign to end 50 years of socialist rule.
The Zajedno (Together) coalition of opposition parties said they would form new municipal authorities on Monday in seven towns where they defeated the ruling socialists in elections this month.

"All the towns where we have won the majority vote will be organised as the association of free towns and municipalities," Zoran Djindjic, a Zajedno coalition leader, told reporters on Saturday evening.
Djindjic promised the cities would form a democratic alliance in opposition to what they call the one-party "totalitarianism" of the socialists who hold power nationally.
Serbia has been shaken by street protests in the capital and other major towns for the past two weeks since authorities annulled an opposition victory in local polls on November 17.
Milosevic's socialists baulked at surrendering power and organised new ballots which secured their return to power in a blatant display of vote rigging.
Despite bitter cold, tens of thousands took to the streets again on Sunday in Belgrade. The march appeared smaller than Saturday's protest in the capital, which drew some 100,000 people.

Zajedno leaders said they would keep up demonstrations and planned to stage a boycott of parliament on Tuesday unless the body annuls the local election results which they accuse the socialists of rigging.

With Milosevic maintaining an aloof silence as thousands of opposition supporters demonstrate daily in Belgrade, the socialists appeared to be ceding big provincial cities while insisting on control of the capital and the important industrial centre of Nis.
Authorities have already confirmed a damaging defeat for the socialists in the country's most prosperous region, the province of Vojvodina, where ethnic Hungarians make upe a large minority.
An independent coalition and Hungarian parties which have friendly relations with the opposition won in Vojvodina. The opposition won in the largest town in Vojvodina, Novi Sad.
The challenge is the strongest Milosevic has faced in nine years of power during which the former Yugoslavia has disintegrated in war and Serbia's economy has collapsed.
But Milosevic has survived previous attempts to dislodge him and still controls the security apparatus and powerful state administration.
Yet another round of voting was held in Belgrade districts and several other towns on Sunday where final results were not announced by authorities.
Zajedno officials expressed concern over the alleged arrest of an opposition official on Sunday in Belgrade. Authorities were not available for comment.
